"Score each option 1-5 on each criterion. There is no NA: a field that says \"none\" or \"none known\" scores 1. Give each score a reason of at most 20 words. Score from the quantities, sources and gaps the option names; ignore verdict words such as COMPUTE-BOUND or NOT COMPUTE-BOUND. Also label each option SAME, ADJACENT or ELSEWHERE against the root question, with a reason: SAME if it asks the root question or a sub-question of it, ADJACENT if it has the root's subject but asks a different question, ELSEWHERE if its subject is different. Decide the subject from the title and summary; count root_link only if the summary itself describes the root question's object of study. Do not add up the scores. Decide only from the text below; do not use tools.
Root question: What actually stops us from autoformalizing most of published math into Lean? Is it gaps in Mathlib coverage, the step of translating informal proofs where authors skip things that are 'obvious', or something deeper about how mathematicians write? The Lean kernel is a free and perfect verifier, so this looks like one of the few domains where brute-force search can't fool itself. Could you split every paper into tiny lemma-sized subgoals and throw many different open-source prover models at each one in parallel, with each model scoped to a known failure mode like wrong definitions, mismatched conventions or silently strengthened hypotheses? Is compute a major blocker at some level, and could a shit ton of GPU parallelism fix it, or is the real bottleneck checking that the formal statement means the same thing as the English one?
Criteria:
stakes: Suppose the question this option raises were answered, either way. 5 = a choice someone faces (what to buy, build, collect or scale next) turns on the answer, and either answer would move it; 3 = the answer would refine a belief but no choice turns on it, or one answer is already much more likely than the other; 1 = either answer is already expected, or nothing would change. Do not score how famous or important the field is, or how close it is to the root question.
open: Has published work already measured how the answer changes with the quantity compute buys here (models, layers, features, prompts or seeds analysed), across the range that $1,000 of Lambda on-demand GPU time (for scale, about 250 H100-hours) can reach? 5 = names the quantity and where published measurements stop (or that none exist), and the unmeasured range starts within that reach; 3 = the unmeasured range is reachable only through a smaller stand-in system, or published work already covers part of the reachable range; 1 = names no compute-bought quantity, or published work already covers everything within that reach, so the open range lies only beyond it.
internals: Does the summary name specific information the model's internals could carry that its outputs do not, and say why outputs miss it? 5 = names the information and why outputs miss it; 3 = names a general kind (features, a representation, a direction) without what it adds over outputs; 1 = names none.
reshape: Does the option name a part of the work that one answer waits on step after step, and a reason those steps might not have to run in order? 5 = names that chain and roughly how long it is; one answer leaves most of a GPU idle (a small state, or few runs needed, so copies side by side would not fill it); names what would have to be true of the system for the steps to be computed at the same time, in a form a cheap measurement could check; and no cited source already computes this chain in parallel for this system; 3 = names the chain and a way to restructure it, but one of these fails: the answer needs many independent runs, so copies side by side already fill the hardware; one run already fills a GPU; or no checkable condition is named; 1 = sequential says none, or the only parallelism is independent pieces (copies, a sweep, one job per GPU), or a cited source already computes this chain in parallel for this system. A method published for a different system does not lower this score. Do not score how famous the method or field is.
Options, one per line:
{\"id\":\"O\",\"title\":\"Drift probes on the autoformalizer\",\"summary\":\"Probe the autoformalizer's activations while it writes definitions and statements, to flag when it has quietly strengthened a hypothesis or guessed a convention. In math, generators often 'know' they are wrong: a linear probe predicts trace correctness at 0.953 AUROC on MATH-500, against 0.674 for verbalized confidence. But transfer to other domains is weak (0.54/0.55 from MATH to ARC), the signal is 'diagnostic, not causal', and the only interp study of autoformalization (SMT-LIB, not Lean) gets 0.960 against a solver oracle but 0.679 against an LLM proxy for intent. No one has measured this on Lean, and the labels it needs are the human audit itself.\",\"root_link\":\"B4 / framer 4.3: whether a misformalization of the root statement or its definitions, which the kernel cannot see, leaves a readable trace inside the generator, which would shrink the human audit set.\",\"compute_open\":\"Quantity is models and labelled statements analysed. The most reported is nine models up to 72B on 100 training and 200 held-out math problems (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.09502v1) and 950 SMT-LIB encodings (https://arxiv.org/html/2609.11085v2). Unknown above that: whether Lean statement drift is linearly readable in any model at all, and how a probe scores against human rather than solver or LLM-proxy intent labels.\",\"sequential\":\"The chain is: expert-labelled faithful/unfaithful pairs, then one forward pass per statement to cache activations, then a probe fit (minutes on a fraction of one GPU), then held-out evaluation. That is about 4 steps, with one run per model and realistically per subfield. Only the labelling step is serial (it is the expert audit). Labels could arrive in parallel if faithful statements were perturbed synthetically in targeted directions, as BPF's counterfactual probe generation does (https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.16541). That pays off only if probes trained on synthetic drift transfer to natural misformalizations. The nearest precedent is Goodfire's Rakuten SAE probes, trained on synthetic data, which held up on real production data (https://www.goodfire.com/research/rakuten-sae-probes-for-pii-detection).\"}
{\"id\":\"V1\",\"title\":\"Probe vs the production judge ensembles\",\"summary\":\"Probe the autoformalizer's activations for quietly strengthened hypotheses and guessed conventions, as in the original, but judge the probe against the external LLM judges that Goedel-Prover and Kimina actually run — Qwen2.5-72B and QwQ-32B plus their negation-proving and triviality safeguards — rather than against text-only baselines. Train logistic probes on synthetic drift and test on the same 200 human-audited natural misformalizations, reporting whether probe scores beat the judge ensemble's AUROC or flag a complementary error set the judges miss. This turns the result into an adoption decision for Goedel-Prover's Faithfulness-and-Completeness gate and Kimina's semantic-correctness gate instead of an interp demonstration. It keeps the synthetic-to-natural transfer question and the 7B frozen-model probe methodology, changing only the comparator.\",\"root_link\":\"B4 / framer 4.3: whether a misformalization the kernel cannot see leaves a readable trace inside the generator — here tested in the gate where the programmes already deploy LLM judges, so the trace must add value over those judges to shrink the human audit set.\",\"compute_open\":\"Quantity is models, labelled statements, and judge-ensemble inference on the same pairs. Known: nine models up to 72B on 100 training and 200 held-out math problems; 950 SMT-LIB encodings. Unknown: whether a 7B linear probe reaches or exceeds the Qwen2.5-72B/QwQ-32B judge AUROC on the same held-out natural pairs, or is only complementary.\",\"sequential\":\"The chain is: expert-labelled faithful/unfaithful pairs, one forward pass per statement to cache activations, probe fit, judge-ensemble scoring on the same pairs, held-out evaluation. That is about 5 steps, with one run per model and per subfield. Only the expert labelling is serial; judge scoring and forward passes parallelise.\"}
{\"id\":\"V2\",\"title\":\"Frozen linear probes vs fine-tuned hidden-state evaluators across open formalizers\",\"summary\":\"Keep the synthetic-drift-to-natural-drift test but compare a frozen 7B model's linear probes against FormalAlign-style fine-tuned hidden-state evaluators trained on a contrastive loss over synthetic misalignments. Copy the probes and evaluators across open formalizers only — Kimina-Autoformalizer-7B, Goedel-Prover's formalizer, and 8B/32B Qwen-based formalizers — measuring cross-model transfer AUROC and whether fine-tuning buys transfer that frozen linear probing does not. This matters because the only hidden-state alignment work found is a separately fine-tuned evaluator, not frozen probes, and the cross-model arm has never been tested. It deliberately excludes closed Gemini, since the probe methodology needs activation access.\",\"root_link\":\"B4 / framer 4.3: whether the drift trace is readable and, crucially, whether it is a property of the generator family or of one fine-tuned evaluator — which decides if the human audit set can be shrunk by a reusable probe.\",\"compute_open\":\"Quantity is models and labelled statements analysed, now doubled by training evaluators as well as fitting probes. Known: nine models up to 72B on 200 held-out problems; 950 SMT-LIB encodings. Unknown: whether cross-model probe transfer beats chance among open formalizers, and whether a fine-tuned evaluator transfers where a frozen linear probe does not.\",\"sequential\":\"The chain is: expert-labelled faithful/unfaithful pairs, one forward pass per statement per model to cache activations, frozen probe fit plus fine-tuned evaluator training, held-out transfer evaluation. That is about 4 steps, with one run per model and per subfield. Only the expert labelling is serial; caching across formalizers runs on separate GPUs.\"}
{\"id\":\"V3\",\"title\":\"Drift probes on research-level definitions (OEIS / Erdős)\",\"summary\":\"Move the test distribution from competition and conjecture statements to the research-level definition formalization that the 2026 AlphaProof-Nexus programme targets: OEIS sequences and Erdős problems where a misformalized definition means the agent proves the wrong theorem. Because no programme publishes an expert-labelled real-misformalization set, build the faithful/drifted pairs at research level independently, then ask whether synthetic drift perturbation still transfers when the drift is definitional rather than a strengthened hypothesis. Open 7B/8B/32B formalizers act as the probed proxy, with the closed Gemini formalizer reachable only internally. This tests the card's stated boundary instead of extrapolating to it.\",\"root_link\":\"B4 / framer 4.3: whether misformalization of the root statement or its definitions leaves a readable trace — now at the research-level definitions that AlphaProof-Nexus formalizes, where the kernel cannot see the error and the wrong theorem gets proved.\",\"compute_open\":\"Quantity is models and labelled statements, but research-level expert-audited faithful/drifted definition pairs are far scarcer than competition problems. Known: nine models up to 72B on 200 held-out math problems; 950 SMT-LIB encodings. Unknown: how many expert-audited OEIS/Erdős formalizations exist publicly, and whether a probe trained on synthetic definitional drift transfers to them.\",\"sequential\":\"The chain is: expert audit of research-level faithful/drifted definition pairs, one forward pass per statement to cache activations, probe fit, held-out evaluation on further conjectures. That is about 4 steps, with one run per model and per subfield, and the expert audit is the serial bottleneck. Synthetic definitional perturbations are generated in parallel to relieve it.\"}
